assumptions: The opportunity begins as a narrow sponsor-funded service for one standardized EEG, sleep, or fatigue protocol rather than attempting to build a broad multi-device CRO at launch.

A qualified principal investigator, clinic coordinator, and privacy or quality owner can be contracted, but their availability, terms, and willingness to accept the required responsibilities are not yet established.

The proposed project prices and gross-margin range are planning estimates; incumbent category presence supports the existence of paid demand but does not validate this offer's prices, costs, conversion, or renewal.
No exclusive clinic capacity, reusable benchmark-data rights, sponsor commitments, or favorable protocol-specific regulatory determination should be assumed until contracted or formally established.

The founder retains the corporate job until the business demonstrates the traction and runway conditions in the founder profile, so the operating model must remain delegable within the stated time limit.
EHDS is treated as a possible longer-term market and infrastructure development, not as a near-term source of exclusive or freely licensable clinical data.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid or sponsor-prepaid pilot for one sharply defined protocol, paired with a costed clinic agreement that assigns qualified responsibilities and grants durable lawful rights to reuse derived benchmarks, plus comparative proof of a material price, speed, cohort-access, or validation-quality advantage and evidence of repeat sponsor demand.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The combination of standardized clinic execution, paired clinician labels, and cross-study benchmark analysis addresses a genuine reproducibility problem and could turn project work into a reusable asset. The insight is credible but not yet distinctive: multiple established providers already integrate protocols, devices, analytics, clinical validation, and participant operations, while the specific unmet Central-European or EEG/sleep gap remains an inference.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Wearable and medical-device teams face consequential validation needs when launching new devices, algorithms, endpoints, or intended uses, and existing wearable-CRO offerings demonstrate a paid category. However, there is no direct evidence that target sponsors will pay this candidate's proposed prices, prepay a first protocol, license its benchmark, or prefer its cohort and protocol over incumbent alternatives, so segment-specific willingness to pay remains uncertain rather than disproven.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Milestone-funded studies can carry meaningful contract values, and benchmark access could add higher-margin repeat revenue if lawful reuse rights and recurring sponsor utility are secured. Against that, the 40%-70% gross-margin range, 18-36 month payback, renewal behavior, project pricing, and owner-earnings path are all unvalidated; clinic labor, recruitment, insurance, equipment, secure processing, regulatory work, and biostatistics create substantial variable cost. The estimated 175,000 PLN launch capital also exceeds the founder's freely available capital before sponsor funding is proven.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: A first protocol for European biosensor teams needing independent EEG, sleep, or fatigue validation is narrower and more actionable than a generic clinical-research offer, and individual contracts could make even a modest beachhead economically relevant. The current definition still spans several customer types, device classes, endpoints, and regulatory routes, with no quantified reachable sponsor set or demonstrated underserved subsegment.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: The intended control point—exclusive repeat clinic capacity plus rights to derived benchmarks—could support a strong niche position if actually contracted. At present neither element exists, while VivoSense, Empatica, TNO, and Delve already cover substantial portions of the proposed end-to-end stack and bring broader capabilities, trust, and operating history. A plausible niche entry does not yet amount to a credible route to dominate it.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful protocol and clinic network could extend to additional device versions, endpoints, biosignals, intended uses, cohorts, and geographies, with prior operating knowledge lowering the cost of later studies. Expansion is meaningfully constrained by protocol-specific approvals, heterogeneous data rights, and the possibility that sponsor-funded datasets cannot be reused across clients, but these are unresolved conditions rather than proof that expansion is unavailable.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Consistent longitudinal protocol data, calibrated failure modes, clinic workflows, and sponsor trust could compound and create switching or replication friction. The proposed durable asset depends on unproven clinic exclusivity and lawful cross-client benchmark reuse, and permit, consent, sponsor, trade-secret, and GDPR constraints can fragment that asset. Well-capitalized incumbents can also reproduce protocols or source cohorts unless the candidate secures genuinely scarce access or data.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Central-European access, a repeat EEG/sleep protocol, and potentially lower cost could matter to some sponsors. No evidence yet quantifies a superior price, cycle time, cohort access, signal quality, regulatory acceptance, or benchmark predictive value, so there is not yet a demonstrated advantage strong enough to change buying behavior away from established providers.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Continued wearable and digital-biomarker development creates recurring validation needs, and regulation reinforces the value of credible evidence and qualified operations. EHDS does not supply a near-term shortcut: its relevant secondary-use provisions phase in later and retain permits, secure environments, fees, and rights protections. Timing is therefore supportive at the category level but offers no clear temporary window unique to this business.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Clinic partnerships could provide repeat participant supply, while focused outreach to device-development teams can in principle produce high-value sponsor relationships. No signed clinic channel, design partner, sponsor pipeline, or repeatable acquisition mechanism is evidenced, and sales will be trust-heavy and likely long-cycle against established CROs. That route is possible but poorly matched to a part-time founder unless domain sales and clinical credibility are deliberately supplied by partners.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's neuroscience and data-science skills fit signal analysis and protocol measurement, and AI can accelerate software, analytics, and documentation. It cannot replace qualified clinical leadership, ethics and regulatory processes, participant safety, privacy and quality ownership, recruitment operations, or institutional relationships. The business therefore depends on several uncommitted specialists and partners, may exceed available capital, and is difficult to operate within the founder's time limit until those responsibilities are contractually delegated.

highest_value_structural_change: Convert the broad foundry into a sponsor-precommitted single-protocol consortium: secure two or more noncompeting device sponsors and one clinic network before launch, have sponsors fund the governed reference cohort, preserve contractually defined cross-sponsor derived-benchmark rights, and standardize a narrow EEG/sleep endpoint where the clinic has scarce recruitment access. This would reduce founder cash exposure, validate distribution and willingness to pay, narrow the regulatory route, and make the benchmark asset harder to replicate.
main_structural_strength: A sponsor-funded validation service can monetize an obligatory, high-consequence job immediately while repeated execution of one stable protocol may compound into a differentiated benchmark and operating asset.
primary_score_limiter: The business has not established an asymmetric control point or measurable buying advantage over mature wearable-CRO competitors; its intended moat depends simultaneously on clinic exclusivity and reusable benchmark rights that are both unproven.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: VivoSense, Empatica, TNO, and Delve already market overlapping end-to-end protocol, device, analytics, clinical-validation, quality-control, regulatory, and participant-operation capabilities, directly weakening the premise that the proposed integrated service is an underserved wedge.
